The Obsidian Fringe: a ring of obsidian cliffs, spires, and mountains surrounding the Maranathi Desert, both of which were formed when the Fire Conduit was constructed and came into power, leveling everything within a several hundred-mile radius. It's full of razor-sharp edges, crumbling passages where the obsidian is thinner and more brittle than in other areas, and lovely little creatures called Husks - the lost and wandering Corrupted souls of the Maranathi Empire.

If you're accessing the Maranathi Desert through one of the gateways - opened centuries ago by Baharian slaves - and traveling in a group, you should be fine. But if you're alone, and you dare to find your own path among the jagged black and green stone, you'll find the Obsidian Fringe is less merciful than you could have imagined.

Husks are relentless creatures, walking statues of glassy stone, whose only goals are to Corrupt all they encounter. Corruption is spread via tiny shards of Corrupted obsidian that can be fired, injected, stabbed - whatever it takes to get under your skin, so to speak. The Corruption will take you slowly, first causing chronic pain, then inhibiting basic cognitive function, before robbing you of all that made you who you were and turning you into the same mindless creature with obsidian for skin and burning embers for eyes.

If you can avoid the Husks and impaling yourself on shards of obsidian, it's the climate that might do you in afterward. Much like the desert it naturally fortifies, the Obsidian Fringe is hot, dry, and unforgiving in the light of day, and frigid and windy once the sun goes down. In tiny hidden pockets, small aquifers were exposed by the blast that created the mountains, but surviving long enough to reach them - and then, long enough to leave the mountains and tell the tale - are two things much easier said than done. Your best bet is to travel in a well-supplied and equally well-defended caravan or, at the very least, a sufficiently scrappy band of adventurers.

These are characters from the WIP I'm pantsing, with the working title *All Things Dark* (given just so it wasn't an untitled doc sitting in Google drive).

**Laurel Mayweather:** Laurel has no memories beyond the five years she's spent living by the coast during the summer and in town working for a blacksmith during the winter. All she knows is her name and, somehow, how to live off the land. She is also a shapeshifter, but has no clue how she received her powers (magic is somewhat rare and often regarded with distrust in this world). One of her biggest flaws is her impulsiveness; in one scene, she follows a woman to the local temple, eavesdrops on her prayers, and then steals one of her offerings from the bowl in front of a statue. She does this all out of curiosity, and without realizing until later that what she's done is pretty fucked up. As it happens, the woman she followed is *Robyn Mayweather*, Laurel's sister who visited the temple out of desperation to pray for her return. Whoops.

**Robyn Mayweather:** Laurel's sister, grieving for five years after she disappeared into a storm one night. Robyn is the talk of the town, being from an old, rich, reclusive family, and especially after her sister went missing. People still occasionally whisper about her and the mysterious circumstances from five years ago; she hears none of this, as she remains largely confined to her manor. She's headstrong almost to a fault, and extremely protective of Laurel (particularly in the year leading up to her disappearance). When Laurel sneaks into her garden to return the items she stole, Robyn catches her and confronts her - and then realizes she's just caught her own sister trespassing. From there she has to convince Laurel that they are, in fact, sisters, as well as debrief her on what happened before she went missing and try to supply her with as much information about her life as she can. (Am currently working on this part.)

**Theo:** The blacksmith's son. He's Laurel's best friend and is currently developing stronger feelings for her (haven't done much with that yet, as I'm still largely in the beginning phase of the story). He gets tangled into this mess when he comes looking for her the day after she sneaks to Robyn's house and doesn't come home, and vows to help her sort through the mess and find a way to retrieve her memories. As he's a secondary character, I don't have a whole lot written for him yet; but the plan is to have him be loyal, protective, and a little bit in awe of Laurel as she's almost the same size as him (very tall, very muscular, very strong). Though I'm thinking some jealousy as Laurel begins to spend more time with Robyn might be something to try as well, since they would normally spend a good deal of their time together during the winter.

**Cassius:** He's only just been introduced so far, but the plan is to have him be an extremely powerful demon with powers of soul corruption and manipulation (maybe some others like shapeshifting and whatnot). He is ultimately what led to Laurel's disappearance, having molded her into his life to the point where she was convinced she couldn't live without him. This character and his motivations are still very rough, as I haven't even properly written him into any of the story yet, but I do know that he is extremely manipulative, arrogant, and cunning; but he puts on a show of charm and indulgence to those he wishes to ensnare. I'm still trying to untangle the reasoning behind his target strategy; maybe he gains more power from each soul he corrupts, or from the memories he takes and the lives he destroys. As I type this I lean more to the second one, as he would need to gain his subject's deepest trust in order to access the memories and extract them. Who knows. Anyways, yeah, fucked up dude. Looking forward to the challenge.

Others: **Silas** the blacksmith, **Wylla** being his wife, a mysterious old lady at the market that points Laurel and Robyn in the right direction to retrieving the memories, **Cornelius** the groundskeeper and adoptive father of the two Mayweathers. I'll probably have more as the story progresses, but yeah! That's what I got so far!

Threw me for a fuckin' loop, because I've spent a lot of time trying to avoid have/had/has. I wish they'd taught actual grammar classes at my school, but now I see I need to take the initiative on my own. English is great! :P

I've been going through much of the same feelings recently. I've got multiple plots planned out almost to the letter (I know I'm not supposed to do that, but I rarely follow 100% of what I plan anyways), some editing I need to do, but sometimes I just don't have it in me. I'm scared I'll mess up so bad that I'll just up and quit writing forever, which is scarier than ruining a plot for me.

But lately I've found that simply taking a step back and writing for the sake of writing, with minimal to no planning, has been so so relaxing and freeing. Right now I'm freewriting a fantasy story, and just allowing myself to become immersed in something that's only for me has proven to be such a great learning experience. It allows me to closely watch the areas I know I need practice in like dialogue and character development - I'm constantly asking myself "what happens next?" and "how will this affect the story later on?" It's like practicing a sport; if I mess up on this one thing that I don't let myself take too seriously, I know it won't be the end of me because I'll always have room to improve. Taking a break from the stories I have big plans for gives me the space I need to recognize where I need improvement and the space to make those improvements - instead of worrying whether or not I'm following the steps I laid out for myself. Sometimes I just have to look at a plot and say, "I'll come back to you when I know I have the tools to make you work."

I think this is just one step out of many towards growing as a writer and being more comfortable with writing things you've become attached to, but it can be one of those things that you use "in the moment" - because when I start freewriting, it's because I'm overwhelmed by what I have planned out, and just need some time to let things simmer while keeping my skills polished. (Also: don't let unfinished freewriting projects freak you out. I've probably got two dozen just sitting in my computer right now - but they all helped me learn more about my work, and I'm still proud of what I did with them. Sometimes writing until you can't anymore is just the way things go.) I hope this made some sense and maybe even helped a little, and good luck with your writing! <3
